The word dummy has several distinct meanings as a noun. Almost all of them share a connecting thread: something that looks like or stands in for the real thing, but isn't fully genuine, functional, or in control. There is also one informal meaning where it describes a person.
1. A stupid or foolish person

In everyday informal speech, calling someone a "dummy" means they are being foolish, slow to understand, or not using their brain well.

  • "I left my keys inside the car — I'm such a dummy!"
  • "Don't be a dummy; just read the instructions."

The tone can range from affectionate and playful (a parent saying it to a child after a silly mistake) to mildly insulting (said in frustration). It is not a deeply harsh insult, but it is informal and casual — you would not write it in a formal letter or a professional email.
2. A life-size model of a human body

A dummy is a human-shaped figure made of plastic, foam, wood, or similar material. It represents a human being and is used as a stand-in when a real person is not needed or not safe.

Tailor's dummy (dressmaker's dummy): A torso-shaped stand used by tailors and fashion designers. Because it holds the exact shape of a human body, a tailor can pin, cut, and adjust clothing on it without making someone stand still for hours.

Crash test dummy: A specially built human-shaped figure used in car safety tests. When engineers need to know how a crash affects the human body, they place these dummies inside the car instead of real people. The dummies are fitted with sensors that measure the force and impact of a collision.

Shop window dummy / display dummy: The full-body figures you see standing in clothing store windows, dressed in outfits. Shoppers look at how the clothes fit the dummy to get an idea of how they would look on a real person.

Ventriloquist's dummy: A puppet built to look like a small person — usually a stylised child or a comic character — used by a ventriloquist (a performer who makes their voice appear to come from somewhere else). The performer's hand goes inside the dummy and controls its moving mouth, making it appear to "talk." The dummy seems to have a personality of its own, but of course it is the performer who is really speaking.
3. A baby's pacifier (British English)

In British, Australian, and Irish English, a dummy is the soft rubber or silicone object placed in a baby's mouth to soothe them. Sucking on it calms the baby even when they are not feeding.

  • "The baby wouldn't stop crying until his mum gave him his dummy."

In American English, the exact same object is called a pacifier (or informally, a binky). This meaning of "dummy" is specific to British-influenced varieties of English, so if you are reading American writing, you will not encounter it.
4. A fake or imitation version of something real

A dummy can be any object designed to look like the real thing, but which is non-functional, inert, or purely decorative. Its job is to deceive, stand in, or fill a space.

  • Dummy security cameras: Fake cameras installed in shops, homes, or buildings to make people think they are being watched. They look identical to real cameras but do not record anything. They are used as a cheaper deterrent against crime.
  • Dummy weapons / dummy ammunition: Replica guns, grenades, or bullets used in military training exercises or in film and theatre productions. They have the appearance of real weapons but cannot fire or cause harm.
  • Dummy pill (placebo): In medical trials, a dummy pill looks exactly like the real medicine being tested but contains no active ingredient. Scientists use it to check whether a drug's effect is real, or whether patients are simply feeling better because they believe they have taken medicine.
  • Dummy book: A rough physical model of a planned book, showing its approximate size, number of pages, and layout. Publishers and authors use it to agree on the design before printing the final version.
  • Dummy invoice / dummy document: A placeholder or practice document that resembles a real one but is not official. Used for testing, training, or demonstration purposes.

The idea is always the same: the dummy looks like the real thing, but it is not the real thing.
5. In the card game Bridge

In Bridge, a two-team card game, the word dummy has a specific technical meaning.

After the bidding phase ends and play begins, one player — called the dummy — lays their entire hand of cards face-up on the table for everyone at the table to see. This player then steps back: their partner plays both hands (their own cards and the dummy's cards) for the rest of that round.

So "the dummy" refers to both the player whose hand is exposed and the exposed hand of cards itself.

  • "After the opening lead, East became the dummy and spread all thirteen cards face-up."

The name fits perfectly: just like a ventriloquist's dummy that appears to act but is really controlled by someone else, the "dummy" player is present at the table but not in control — their partner acts for them.
6. In football (soccer) and rugby — a dummy move

In football and rugby, a dummy is a deliberate act of deception during play. A player pretends to pass, shoot, or receive the ball — makes all the body movements suggesting they are about to do something — but then does not actually do it, letting the ball roll past them or pulling out at the last second. The opposing player, fooled by the fake movement, reacts to something that never happened, and this gives the player an advantage.

The common phrases are:

  • to sell a dummy — to successfully deceive an opponent with a fake move
  • to buy a dummy — to be deceived by a fake move
  • "He sold the defender a brilliant dummy and burst through the gap."

Here, "a dummy" as a noun refers to the deceptive fake move itself.
7. In computing, statistics, and programming — a placeholder

In technical fields, a dummy is something that fills a required slot but does not carry any real content or perform any real function. It is a stand-in used during development, testing, or analysis.

  • Dummy variable (statistics): A variable used to represent categories numerically. For example, to represent whether someone passed or failed a test, you might use a dummy variable: 1 means "passed," 0 means "failed." It is a simple number that stands in for a real-world category.
  • Dummy data: Fake, randomly generated data used to test a software system before real data is available. Instead of filling a database with actual customer information during development, programmers use dummy data so they can test how the system behaves.
  • Dummy function / dummy argument: A placeholder function or piece of code that occupies a required position in a program but does not yet do anything meaningful. Developers use it while building and testing.
Pulling it all together

Look across all these meanings and one idea appears again and again:

A dummy is something (or someone) that stands in for the real thing — it resembles it, fills its role, or takes its place — but it is not the genuine article.

  • A tailor's dummy stands in for a person's body.
  • A crash test dummy takes a human's place in a dangerous test.
  • A dummy camera looks like a real camera but does nothing.
  • A dummy pill looks like medicine but contains nothing active.
  • A dummy variable stands in for a real-world category.
  • The Bridge dummy is present but not really in charge.
  • A sporting dummy is a fake action designed to look like a real one.

The one meaning that sits slightly apart is calling a person a dummy (meaning foolish) — but even here, the suggestion is that they are not performing as a fully capable, alert person would.
One older, now-rare meaning

Historically — and you may come across this in old books or films — "dummy" was also used to refer to a person who could not speak (a mute person). This usage is now considered offensive and outdated. You are unlikely to encounter it in modern everyday language, but it is worth knowing exists in case you see it in older texts.
Register and usage — a quick guide

• Calling a person a dummy (stupid) = informal, casual; can be playful or mildly insulting; avoid in formal contexts.
  • Dummy = pacifier is British/Australian/Irish English only; in American English, this meaning does not exist.
  • All other meanings (mannequin, fake object, placeholder, Bridge term, sports move) are neutral and perfectly appropriate in everyday and professional speech or writing.
